title: Why Does My Dog Eat Grass?
excerpt: Grass-eating is one of the most common — and most misunderstood — dog habits. Here's what the evidence actually says, and the handful of signs that mean it's worth a vet visit.

sections.heading: The short answer: it's usually normal
paragraphs: If your dog stops mid-walk to graze like a small, enthusiastic cow, you are in very good company. Surveys of dog owners consistently find that eating plants is common in healthy dogs, and that most of them do it without any obvious ill effects.

Grass-eating is often filed under "pica" — eating non-food items — but it doesn't behave much like a problem. Most dogs who eat grass do it now and then, chew a bit, swallow, and carry on with their day. It's closer to a quirk than a symptom.

That said, "usually normal" is not the same as "always fine". The useful skill is knowing which pattern you're looking at, and that comes down to how often it happens, how frantic it looks, and what else is going on with your dog.

sections.heading: The sick-dog theory, and why it's only half true
paragraphs: The most repeated explanation is that dogs eat grass to make themselves sick, either to clear an upset stomach or to bring up something that shouldn't be there. There's a grain of truth here, but it's smaller than the folklore suggests.

When researchers have asked owners about their dogs' grass-eating, the majority reported that their dog did not seem unwell beforehand and did not vomit afterwards. In other words, vomiting is the exception rather than the rule. If dogs were using grass as a deliberate emetic, you'd expect the sick bit to happen far more often than it does.

There is a more plausible version of this theory: grass may sometimes be a response to a vague, nauseous, grumbly feeling rather than a plan to vomit. Some dogs with reflux, nausea or gut discomfort do gulp grass quickly and urgently — and that pattern, the frantic one, is worth paying attention to. The relaxed, browsing, nibbling-the-good-bits-at-the-edge-of-the-path pattern is a different animal entirely.
So: don't panic every time your dog eats grass, but do notice if it comes with lip-licking, drooling, swallowing repeatedly, refusing food or repeated vomiting.

sections.heading: The more likely explanations
paragraphs: Ancestry and instinct. Wild canids eat plant material — it shows up routinely in analyses of wolf and fox scat. Dogs may simply be doing something their relatives have always done, without needing a medical reason for it. Grass-eating is a normal part of the canine behavioural repertoire.

It tastes good. Fresh spring grass is sweet, cool and damp. Dogs are opportunistic eaters, and new growth after rain is genuinely appealing. Many owners notice their dog grazes far more in April than in November, which fits taste and texture better than it fits illness.

Fibre and gut feel. Grass adds bulk and roughage. Some individual dogs may graze more when their digestion is sluggish or their stools are loose, and a handful of case reports describe grass-eating that stopped once the diet changed. This isn't proof that grass fixes anything, but fibre is a reasonable thing to discuss with your vet if your dog is a very keen grazer.

Boredom and habit. This one is underrated. A dog left in the garden with nothing to do will investigate the only available entertainment, which is often the lawn. Grazing can also become a reliable way of getting your attention — if every nibble triggers a dramatic "no, leave it!", you have accidentally made grass interesting.
Appetite and routine. Some dogs graze more before meals, on an empty stomach, which hints at hunger or anticipation rather than illness.

sections.heading: When grass-eating isn't harmless
paragraphs: The grass itself is rarely the problem. What's on it or near it can be.

Lawn treatments. Herbicides, fertilisers, slug pellets and pesticides are the main risk. Keep dogs off treated lawns for as long as the product label specifies, and be cautious about verges and municipal parks where you don't know what's been sprayed.

Parasites. Grass in areas used by other dogs, foxes, slugs and snails can carry parasite stages, including lungworm, which is spread via slugs and snails and can be serious. Keep parasite prevention up to date and talk to your vet about lungworm cover if you're in an affected area.

Grass seeds. In late spring and summer, barbed grass seeds are a genuine nuisance — they can lodge in ears, paws, eyes and, occasionally, the mouth and throat. A dog that suddenly starts gagging, pawing at its face or shaking its head after a grassy walk needs checking.
Toxic plants. The bigger risk is a dog who grazes indiscriminately and hoovers up bulbs, daffodils, foxgloves, yew or mushrooms along with the grass. Know what's growing in your garden.
Volume. A dog who eats grass in large, compulsive quantities, or who also eats soil, stones, fabric or faeces, has moved beyond ordinary grazing and deserves a proper look.

sections.heading: What to do about it today
paragraphs: If your dog is well, eating normally, keeping weight on and grazing casually, the honest answer is: nothing. Let them nibble in places you know haven't been treated.

If you'd rather they didn't, work with the behaviour rather than against it. Teach a cheerful "leave it" and "this way", and pay well for it — a reward your dog actually wants, delivered quickly, beats a telling-off every time. Walk on lead through areas you can't vouch for. Increase sniffing time, chew opportunities and mental work at home so the lawn isn't the most interesting thing available.

Keep a short note of when it happens: time of day, before or after meals, season, and whether vomiting follows. Two weeks of notes will tell you more than any amount of guesswork, and it's genuinely useful information for your vet.

Finally, check the basics. Is your dog getting enough food for their size and activity? Is mealtime timing leaving a very long empty gap? Small adjustments here sometimes settle a grazing habit without any further intervention.

vetNote: Book a vet appointment if grass-eating is new, sudden and frantic; if it comes with repeated vomiting, diarrhoea, drooling, lip-licking, loss of appetite, weight loss or lethargy; if your dog also eats non-food items like stones, soil or fabric; or if you suspect they've eaten a treated lawn, a toxic plant or mushrooms. Seek urgent care for persistent retching without producing anything, a swollen or tense abdomen, collapse, or constant gagging, head-shaking or pawing at the face after a walk in long grass, which can suggest a lodged grass seed.
question: Why does my dog eat grass?

thread.text:
Your dog eats grass. The internet says it's because they feel sick. The internet is mostly wrong 🌱

When owners have been surveyed about this, the majority said their dog seemed perfectly well beforehand — and didn't vomit afterwards.

So what's actually going on?

Most likely: it's just normal dog behaviour.

Wild canids eat plant material too. Fresh spring grass is sweet, cool and damp. Dogs are opportunists. Many owners notice grazing spikes in April and vanishes in November — that fits taste, not illness.

The pattern matters more than the habit.

Relaxed browsing, nibbling the good bits, carrying on with the walk = fine.

Frantic gulping, plus lip-licking, drooling, off food or repeated vomiting = worth a vet call. That's the version to take seriously.

The grass is rarely the problem. What's on it can be.

Lawn treatments and slug pellets. Barbed grass seeds in summer ears and paws. Lungworm via slugs and snails. Daffodil bulbs and mushrooms hoovered up alongside.

Know your patch, keep parasite cover current.

If your dog is well and grazing casually, you can genuinely just... let them.

If you'd rather they didn't: pay generously for a cheerful "leave it", lead through unknown verges, and give them something better to do than the lawn.
